name: Old Waverley Hotel
description: This seven-storey Victorian building on Princes Street, opposite the gardens and Waverley Station, dates from 1848 and was designed by the architect John Armstrong for the hotelier Robert Cranston. With 86 rooms, it was one of the largest hotels on the street when it opened, and it kept the Cranston family's management for decades, giving the building its long-standing local nickname long before "Old Waverley" became its formal name.
interesting_fact: For almost 25 years the hotel operated as "Cranston's Temperance Hotel" - the first temperance hotel in Scotland, serving no alcohol at all at a time when the temperance movement was a serious social and political force across Victorian Britain. Robert Cranston was a committed temperance campaigner as well as a hotelier, and his teetotal Princes Street establishment became a well-known statement in a city otherwise thick with taverns and licensed hotels, before the business eventually dropped the temperance policy and became the more conventional hotel operating under the Old Waverley name today.

name: Museum on the Mound
description: This free museum occupies part of the Bank of Scotland's original headquarters, a grand building designed by Robert Reid and Richard Crichton and built between 1802 and 1806 at a cost of £43,000 for a bank that was already, by then, over a century old - founded in 1695 as Scotland's first bank, and in 1696 the first commercial bank in Europe to issue paper banknotes. The museum itself opened in 2006, two years before the global financial crisis it now can't help but be read through, and covers the story of money and banking through historic banknotes (including Scotland's oldest surviving note), an interactive 1820s life-assurance display, exhibits on financial crime and security, and raised maps tracing the Old Town's development since the 1600s.
interesting_fact: The building has never stopped being a working bank headquarters even while housing a museum - it remains the Scottish headquarters of Lloyds Banking Group today, meaning visitors touring 300 years of banking history are doing so inside an active modern bank building, not a retired one.

name: Assembly Hall
description: This neo-Gothic hall, designed by David Bryce in 1858, sits directly east of Edinburgh Castle atop the Mound and has served since 1929 as the meeting place for the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland - the church's annual governing gathering. It was built for the Free Church of Scotland in the wake of the 1843 Disruption, when a large breakaway movement split from the established Church and urgently needed its own theological college, assembly hall and church nearby. One of its most historically significant moments came in 1910, when 1,355 delegates gathered here for the World Missionary Conference, an event widely credited as the starting point of the modern ecumenical movement. Between 1999 and 2004 it took on an entirely different role, hosting the newly reconvened Scottish Parliament while the purpose-built Holyrood building was under construction.
interesting_fact: Today, for three weeks every August, this same hall housing Scotland's national church assembly transforms into one of the Edinburgh Festival Fringe's most prestigious venues, hosting circus, comedy, music and dance across three separate performance spaces inside it.

name: Edinburgh City Relief Map
description: Set into the pavement on the Mound, this bronze high-relief model reproduces central Edinburgh in miniature - from Lothian Road in the west to Regent Road in the east, and from Queen Street in the north down to the Cowgate in the south - with the Castle, Calton Hill, Waverley Station and Princes Street Gardens all rendered in raised bronze detail, alongside raised lettering naming the major streets. It was presented to the City of Edinburgh in 1984 by the staff of the Edinburgh branch of Marks & Spencer to mark the company's centenary, but its real purpose is tactile rather than decorative: the whole point of casting the city in high relief was to let visitors with visual impairments explore the shape and grandeur of Edinburgh's skyline entirely by touch.
interesting_fact: Because it's designed to be touched rather than just looked at, decades of hands tracing the Castle Rock, the Mound and the major streets have left the bronze polished to a bright golden sheen in exactly those spots, while the rest of the map has darkened naturally with age - a map that visibly records where people actually explore it most.
